draft.title: Progressive overload
card: Progressive overload means gradually increasing the training load over time. The body adapts to the load it is given, so a load that never changes stops causing new gains.
how often the person trains, such as going from two sessions a week to three.
how hard each session is, such as a heavier weight or a faster running pace.
how long each session lasts, such as a 20 minute run becoming a 30 minute run. The increase should be small and steady, as a jump that is too big can lead to injury.
draft.remember: Raise the load a little at a time, and the body keeps adapting.

a.q: Why does a runner who always runs the same route at the same pace stop improving?
opts: The body has adapted, so the load no longer drives new gains
The body can only adapt to a load for a few weeks in total
The route is too short to train the body in any way
A steady pace cannot train the body at all
a.why: The body adapts to the load it is given. Once it has adapted, the same load causes no new gains, so the load must rise. The body does not stop adapting for good: it keeps adapting when the load is increased in small steps.
a.clue: Think about what the body does when a load stays the same.

b.q: Priya has lifted 40 kg for three sets of eight, three times a week, for two months. It now feels easy. Which change follows progressive overload?
opts: Lift 42.5 kg for the same sets and sessions
Lift 60 kg for the same sets and sessions
Lift 40 kg for the same sets and sessions
Lift 40 kg but cut the sessions to one a week
b.why: A small rise in weight increases intensity, and the body can adapt to it. A jump to 60 kg is too big and risks injury. Keeping 40 kg adds no new load, and fewer sessions lowers the load.
b.clue: The increase should be small and steady, not large.

a.best: The body has adapted, so the load no longer drives new gains

b.best: Lift 42.5 kg for the same sets and sessions
